blogs.title: When Expert Testimony Collapses: The Fatal Flaw in Finesse Wireless v. AT&T
blogs.description: This post analyzes the Federal Circuit's reversal of the infringement verdict based primarily on the inadequacy of Dr. Wells' expert testimony regarding the '134 patent. It explores the court's strict application of the 'substantial evidence' standard when an expert offers self-contradictory testimony that requires the jury to engage in significant speculation to bridge gaps. The analysis highlights how a failure to clearly map claim limitations to accused device features—even via complex technical diagrams—can lead to immediate JMOL, reinforcing the principle that an expert cannot pivot mid-testimony without losing credibility.

blogs.title: Prosecution History Estoppel vs. Claim Construction: Did Finesse Surrender Scope Over Two Signals?
blogs.description: Focusing on the '775 patent, this article examines the Federal Circuit's nuanced treatment of prosecution history estoppel and claim construction limits. While rejecting AT&T's argument that amending claims from 'two or three' to 'three' signaled a surrender of scope for devices using two unique signals, the court nonetheless reversed on damages grounds due to a lack of evidence regarding the specific 'seven multiplications.' This piece discusses the tension between broadening claim language during prosecution and the evidentiary burden required at trial to prove literal infringement, particularly when the accused device performs fewer distinct mathematical operations than explicitly claimed.

blogs.title: The Domino Effect: How Non-Infringement Rulings Automatically Vacate Massive Damage Awards
blogs.description: This commentary looks at the procedural efficiency and finality achieved by reversing a JMOL denial on infringement grounds and subsequently vacating a $166 million damages award. Unlike cases where remand is necessary for retrial on liability, *Finesse Wireless* demonstrates how a complete lack of substantial evidence for infringement renders any damages calculation moot. The post considers why courts prefer this approach over ordering new trials on damages alone and what this means for plaintiffs attempting to recover based solely on theory rather than concrete, admissible evidence linking technology to every step of a patented method.
